title: Introduction and Architecture
content:
Overview In an e-commerce application, placing an order triggers several downstream tasks: recording the order, sending a confirmation email, and notifying administrators. If all of these are handled within the same request (synchronously), the system slows down easily as order volume grows, and a failure in a secondary service can cause lost orders or duplicate emails.
This workshop builds an order-processing flow that is event-driven, fault-tolerant, and observable on AWS, then runs measurements to compare it against a synchronous approach.
What you will do Decouple order intake from order processing using Amazon SQS and a dead-letter queue (DLQ) Prevent duplicate processing with Amazon DynamoDB (idempotency) Orchestrate the email and notification workflow with AWS Step Functions, Amazon SES, and Amazon SNS Monitor the system and receive alerts with Amazon CloudWatch Simulate failures and load to evaluate the effectiveness of the architecture Architecture Evaluation metrics Response time of the order API (average, p95) Rate of orders lost when failures occur Number of duplicate emails sent Time from when a failure occurs until an administrator receives an alert Duration and cost Approximately 2–3 hours. Most services fall within the free tier or incur very low costs at test scale. Be sure to perform the cleanup step at the end to avoid incurring charges.

title: Proposal
content:
Design and Implementation of a Fault-Tolerant, Monitored Event-Driven Order Processing Architecture on AWS, with Experimental Evaluation 1. Background and Problem When a customer places an order in an online store, the system has to do several things: record the order, send a confirmation email, update its status, and alert the operator if something goes wrong. The simplest approach is to cram all of this into a single request (synchronous processing). It is easy to write, but it shows four weaknesses once the system runs for real:
Weakness Symptom Slow responses The customer waits for the entire processing chain, especially when a secondary service (such as email) is slow or rate-limited Lost or stuck orders A failing secondary step fails the whole request, and the order may stop in a half-finished state Duplicate processing The customer clicks submit several times, or the system retries on its own, so one order is processed and emailed multiple times Undetected failures Without monitoring, the operator only finds out when customers complain This project proposes an event-driven architecture on AWS to address these weaknesses, then uses experiments to measure where it is better than the synchronous approach and what trade-offs it brings.
2. Objectives and Scope Objectives
Design and deploy an asynchronous order-processing flow that is fault tolerant, free of duplicate processing, and able to raise alerts. Build a synchronous approach as a baseline, running under the same conditions. Measure and compare the two approaches using quantitative metrics. Write workshop documentation so that others can reproduce it step by step. Scope: the system runs in the Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1 region, is deployed with AWS SAM, and is tested at loads of 20 and 50 orders. The project does not build a customer-facing web interface, does not handle payments, and does not aim to measure production-scale performance.
3. Proposed Architecture 3.1. Processing flow The customer sends an order to API Gateway (HTTP API); a Lambda function validates the API key and the order format, puts the order into an SQS queue, and immediately returns 202 Accepted. Another Lambda function reads the message from SQS, records the order in DynamoDB (RECEIVED) using a condition that only writes if the order ID does not yet exist, then starts a Step Functions execution named after the order ID. The state machine sends a confirmation email to the customer through Amazon SES, with exponential-backoff retries. On success: update the status to DONE. On failure after retries are exhausted: update the status to FAILED, send an alert through Amazon SNS, and end in a failed state. CloudWatch monitors the entire flow and raises alerts when something abnormal happens. 3.2. Role of each component Component Service Role Entry point API Gateway, Lambda Receive orders, validate them, respond quickly Queue Amazon SQS Decouple order intake from processing, buffer when order volume rises Dead-letter queue SQS DLQ Hold messages that cannot be processed after the maximum receive count Order ledger Amazon DynamoDB Record the status of each order, prevent duplicate processing Orchestration AWS Step Functions Manage each step, with explicit retries and error catching Notification Amazon SES, Amazon SNS Send email to customers and alerts to administrators Monitoring Amazon CloudWatch Alarms and dashboard Deployment AWS SAM (CloudFormation) Describe the whole infrastructure in a single template 4. Fault-Tolerant Design Each type of failure has its own handling mechanism, rather than relying on one generic mechanism:
Failure Handling mechanism Result Malformed message, Lambda error SQS redelivers the message; after 3 receives it moves to the DLQ No message is lost, and it can be inspected and reprocessed The same order submitted several times Conditional write to DynamoDB; execution name equals the order ID An order runs only once, with no second email Temporary email failure (for example SES rate limiting) Step Functions Retry: 6 attempts, backoff rate 2, with jitter Recovers automatically without intervention Permanent email failure Catch routes to MarkFailed and then NotifyAdminFailure The order is marked FAILED and the administrator is notified immediately 5. Monitoring and Alerting The system has three CloudWatch Alarms: messages in the DLQ, a failed Step Functions execution, and Lambda errors. All three send alerts through the same SNS topic. In addition, a dashboard shows queue length, age of the oldest message, Lambda invocations and errors, and Step Functions executions on a single screen, so the operator can see the state of the system at a glance.
6. Experiment Plan Both approaches are deployed in the same stack and use the same API key so that the comparison is fair:
Synchronous (baseline) Asynchronous (proposed) Endpoint POST /sync POST /async How it processes Writes to DynamoDB and then sends via SES within the request Puts the order into SQS, processed in the background by Lambda and Step Functions Duplicate protection, retries, DLQ, alerts No Yes Three experiments
Latency and load: send 20 and 50 orders with several concurrent requests, and measure API response time (average, p95), the number of completed, failed, stuck, or lost orders, and processing completion time. Duplicates: send the same order ID 5 times to each endpoint and count the extra emails. Failures and alerts: use an unverified email so SES rejects it, measure the time from the failure to the alert (directly through SNS and through the CloudWatch Alarm), and check that malformed messages move to the DLQ. Evaluation metrics: average and p95 API response; rate of lost or stuck orders when failures occur; number of duplicate emails; time until an alert is raised on failure; processing completion time; and the actual cost of the whole experiment.
7. Constraints and Risks Constraint or risk Mitigation The SES sandbox limits sending to 1 email/second and only to verified addresses Use the success@simulator.amazonses.com mailbox simulator, cap the load at 20 and 50 orders, and record this as a bottleneck shared by both approaches Two API endpoints exposed to the Internet Protect them with an x-api-key key, keep the key and samconfig.toml out of the repository, and delete the whole stack when finished Measurements fluctuate because of Lambda cold starts and time of day Warm up first, repeat each load level at least 3 times, and take the average Unexpected costs Set up AWS Budgets from the start, clean up resources at the end, and check Cost Explorer after 1 to 2 days 8. Expected Results An order-processing system running on AWS, repeatably deployable with a single sam deploy command. No order is lost when a step fails; failed orders are retained and trigger an alert. An order is processed and emailed only once, even if it is submitted multiple times. A table of real measurements comparing the two approaches, with an honest discussion of strengths and limitations, including the metrics where the asynchronous architecture has no advantage (for example, completion time is usually longer because processing runs in the background). A step-by-step workshop guide covering preparation, SQS and DLQ, duplicate protection, Step Functions, monitoring, experiments, and cleanup. Future work: add a mechanism to reprocess FAILED orders (currently, resubmitting the same ID is treated as a duplicate), and request that SES be moved out of the sandbox to test at larger loads.
9. Duration and Cost The workshop takes about 2 to 3 hours. At test scale, most services fall within the free tier or cost very little; the actual cost will be recorded from Cost Explorer after the run. Set up a cost alert (AWS Budgets) from the start and perform the resource cleanup step at the end to avoid unexpected charges.

title: Queues and DLQ
content:
Objective Create a main queue that receives orders and a dead-letter queue (DLQ) to keep messages that fail processing, instead of losing them.
Three concepts to remember:
Visibility timeout: the time a message stays hidden after a consumer receives it. If the consumer does not delete the message within this time, the message becomes visible again so it can be retried. maxReceiveCount: the number of times a message can be received without being deleted before it is moved to the DLQ. DLQ: a queue that holds failed messages so they can be inspected and reprocessed. 1. Create the template.yaml file In the order-system folder, create a file named template.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09' Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31 Description: Order workshop - SQS and DLQ Resources: OrdersDLQ: Type: AWS::SQS::Queue Properties: MessageRetentionPeriod: 1209600 # keep failed messages for 14 days OrdersQueue: Type: AWS::SQS::Queue Properties: VisibilityTimeout: 60 RedrivePolicy: deadLetterTargetArn: !GetAtt OrdersDLQ.Arn maxReceiveCount: 3 Outputs: QueueUrl: Value: !Ref OrdersQueue DlqUrl: Value: !Ref OrdersDLQ 2. Deploy sam build sam deploy --guided Answer the prompts as follows:
Prompt Answer Stack Name order-system AWS Region ap-southeast-1 Confirm changes before deploy N Allow SAM CLI IAM role creation Y Disable rollback N Save arguments to samconfig.toml Y When it finishes, SAM prints QueueUrl and DlqUrl.
3. Verify in the Console Go to Amazon SQS → Queues. You will see two queues whose names start with order-system-. Open the main queue → Dead-letter queue tab: the dead-letter queue is attached, with Maximum receives = 3. 4. Test a message falling into the DLQ Store the two queue URLs in variables:
$q = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='QueueUrl'].OutputValue" --output text $dlq = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='DlqUrl'].OutputValue" --output text Send a test message:
aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body "test-dlq" Receive the message several times without deleting it (the --visibility-timeout 0 parameter makes the message visible again immediately):
1..4 | ForEach-Object { aws sqs receive-message --queue-url $q --visibility-timeout 0 --wait-time-seconds 2 Start-Sleep -Seconds 1 } The first three attempts return the message, and the fourth returns nothing. Wait about a minute, then check the DLQ:
aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url $dlq --attribute-names ApproximateNumberOfMessages Or go to the Console → the DLQ queue → Send and receive messages → Poll for messages.
SQS metrics are approximate and may be delayed by several tens of seconds.
Verify the result There are two queues, and the main queue points to the DLQ with maxReceiveCount = 3. A message received more than 3 times without being deleted ends up in the DLQ.

title: Preventing Duplicate Processing
content:
Objective An SQS queue guarantees at-least-once delivery, which means the same order may occasionally be delivered twice. If this is not handled, customers will receive duplicate emails. We use DynamoDB as a “ledger”: each orderId is processed only once. This technique is called idempotency.
1. Update template.yaml Add a DynamoDB table and a Lambda function to template.yaml. Keep OrdersDLQ and OrdersQueue as they are, and replace the rest as follows:
OrdersTable: Type: AWS::DynamoDB::Table Properties: BillingMode: PAY_PER_REQUEST AttributeDefinitions: - AttributeName: orderId AttributeType: S KeySchema: - AttributeName: orderId KeyType: HASH ProcessOrderFn: Type: AWS::Serverless::Function Properties: Handler: index.handler Runtime: nodejs22.x CodeUri: src/ Timeout: 10 Environment: Variables: TABLE_NAME: !Ref OrdersTable Policies: - DynamoDBCrudPolicy: TableName: !Ref OrdersTable Events: FromSqs: Type: SQS Properties: Queue: !GetAtt OrdersQueue.Arn BatchSize: 1 Outputs: QueueUrl: Value: !Ref OrdersQueue DlqUrl: Value: !Ref OrdersDLQ TableName: Value: !Ref OrdersTable The queue’s VisibilityTimeout (60 seconds) is several times larger than the Lambda Timeout (10 seconds). This is the recommended configuration when Lambda reads from SQS.
2. Write the Lambda code Create the file src/index.mjs:
import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb"; import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, PutCommand } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb"; const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({})); export const handler = async (event) => { for (const record of event.Records) { const order = JSON.parse(record.body); // invalid JSON throws an error -> retry -> DLQ try { await db.send(new PutCommand({ TableName: process.env.TABLE_NAME, Item: { orderId: order.orderId, status: "PROCESSING", createdAt: Date.now(), }, // Only write if the orderId does not exist yet ConditionExpression: "attribute_not_exists(orderId)", })); } catch (e) { if (e.name === "ConditionalCheckFailedException") { console.log("Duplicate order, skipping:", order.orderId); continue; } throw e; } console.log("Processed:", order.orderId); } }; The key point is the ConditionExpression: DynamoDB only allows the write if the orderId does not already exist, so the second write is rejected and the Lambda skips that order.
In section 5.5 we will add an order status (PROCESSING → DONE) to handle the case where the order was recorded in the ledger but the email-sending step failed.
3. Redeploy sam build sam deploy 4. Test Get the variables you need:
$q = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='QueueUrl'].OutputValue" --output text $dlq = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='DlqUrl'].OutputValue" --output text $table = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='TableName'].OutputValue" --output text Create the order message file:
'{"orderId":"A001"}' | Out-File -Encoding ascii msg1.json Case 1: valid order
aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body file://msg1.json aws dynamodb scan --table-name $table The DynamoDB table has one row A001 with status = PROCESSING.
Case 2: sending the same order twice
aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body file://msg1.json sam logs --stack-name order-system --name ProcessOrderFn --tail The log shows the line Duplicate order, skipping: A001. Press Ctrl+C to exit log tailing mode. The DynamoDB table still has only one A001 row.
Case 3: a faulty message goes to the DLQ
aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body "not-json" The Lambda fails at JSON.parse, and SQS retries every 60 seconds. After about 3 to 4 minutes, the message appears in the DLQ (Console → DLQ → Poll for messages).
Verify the result Case Expected result Valid order One row in DynamoDB Duplicate send The log reports a duplicate, no new row is added Message that is not JSON After a few retries, the message ends up in the DLQ Troubleshooting Lambda does not run: go to Console → Lambda → the ProcessOrderFn function → Configuration → Triggers tab, and check that the SQS trigger is Enabled. DynamoDB permission error: check the log, and make sure the Policies section of the template uses the correct !Ref OrdersTable. sam logs shows nothing: wait a few seconds and send the message again, as logs have a small delay.

title: Orchestration and Notifications
content:
Objective Instead of letting a single Lambda function do everything, we use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the order-processing workflow. Each step has clear Retry and Catch behavior, the state of every order is recorded, and administrators are notified immediately through Amazon SNS when an order fails.
Workflow:
Lambda receives a message from SQS, records it in DynamoDB (RECEIVED), and starts the state machine. The state machine sends a confirmation email to the customer using Amazon SES (up to 3 retries). On success: update the status to DONE. On failure: update the status to FAILED, send an alert through SNS, and end in a failed state. 1. Check the execution in Step Functions.', $.orderId)" ResultPath: null Next: OrderFailed OrderFailed: Type: Fail Error: OrderProcessingFailed Cause: Could not send the confirmation email ProcessOrderFn: Type: AWS::Serverless::Function Properties: Handler: index.handler Runtime: nodejs22.x CodeUri: src/ Timeout: 10 Environment: Variables: TABLE_NAME: !Ref OrdersTable STATE_MACHINE_ARN: !Ref OrderStateMachine Policies: - DynamoDBCrudPolicy: TableName: !Ref OrdersTable - StepFunctionsExecutionPolicy: StateMachineName: !GetAtt OrderStateMachine.Name Events: FromSqs: Type: SQS Properties: Queue: !GetAtt OrdersQueue.Arn BatchSize: 1 Outputs: QueueUrl: Value: !Ref OrdersQueue DlqUrl: Value: !Ref OrdersDLQ TableName: Value: !Ref OrdersTable StateMachineArn: Value: !Ref OrderStateMachine The ses:SendEmail permission uses Resource: "*" for simplicity in a test environment. In a real environment, restrict it to the sender’s identity.
2. Replace the entire src/index.mjs import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb"; import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, PutCommand, GetCommand, } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb"; import { SFNClient, StartExecutionCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-sfn"; const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({})); const sfn = new SFNClient({}); export const handler = async (event) => { for (const record of event.Records) { const order = JSON.parse(record.body); // invalid JSON -> error -> retry -> DLQ // Step 1: write to the ledger; each orderId may only be written once try { await db.send(new PutCommand({ TableName: process.env.TABLE_NAME, Item: { orderId: order.orderId, status: "RECEIVED", createdAt: Date.now() }, ConditionExpression: "attribute_not_exists(orderId)", })); } catch (e) { if (e.name !== "ConditionalCheckFailedException") throw e; const { Item } = await db.send(new GetCommand({ TableName: process.env.TABLE_NAME, Key: { orderId: order.orderId }, })); if (Item?.status !== "RECEIVED") { console.log("Duplicate order, skipping:", order.orderId); continue; } // Still in RECEIVED state: the previous attempt failed to start the workflow -> retry } // Step 2: start the workflow. The execution name = orderId, so it cannot run twice. try { await sfn.send(new StartExecutionCommand({ stateMachineArn: process.env.STATE_MACHINE_ARN, name: order.orderId, input: JSON.stringify(order), })); console.log("Workflow started:", order.orderId); } catch (e) { if (e.name === "ExecutionAlreadyExists") { console.log("Workflow already exists, skipping:", order.orderId); continue; } throw e; } } }; Because orderId is used as the execution name, it should only contain letters, digits, -, and _ (up to 80 characters).
3. Deploy sam build sam deploy --guided Keep the same answers as last time. When asked for the two parameters, enter:
Parameter Value SenderEmail The email verified in section 5.2 AdminEmail The email that receives alerts (can be the same email as above) Confirm the SNS subscription: AWS sends an email titled AWS Notification - Subscription Confirmation to AdminEmail. Open the email and click Confirm subscription, otherwise you will not receive alerts.
4. Testing Get the variables you need:
$q = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='QueueUrl'].OutputValue" --output text $table = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='TableName'].OutputValue" --output text $email = "your-verified-email@example.com" Case 1: successful order
@{ orderId = "B001"; customerEmail = $email } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress | Out-File -Encoding ascii msg-b001.json aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body file://msg-b001.json Verify:
Your inbox receives the email Order confirmation B001. Go to Step Functions → State machines → select the state machine → the execution named B001 → status Succeeded. Open Graph view to see the steps in green. aws dynamodb scan --table-name $table shows B001 with status = DONE. Case 2: duplicate order
aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body file://msg-b001.json sam logs --stack-name order-system --name ProcessOrderFn --tail The log shows Duplicate order, skipping: B001, and no second email is sent. Press Ctrl+C to exit.
Case 3: email sending failure
Use an address that is not verified in SES. Because the account is in sandbox mode, SES will reject it:
@{ orderId = "B002"; customerEmail = "unverified@example.com" } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress | Out-File -Encoding ascii msg-b002.json aws sqs send-message --queue-url $q --message-body file://msg-b002.json Wait about 20 to 30 seconds (3 retries spaced 2, 4, and 8 seconds apart), then check:
The B002 execution is in Failed status. In Graph view, the SendCustomerEmail step shows an error, and the flow goes through MarkFailed and NotifyAdminFailure. The alert email Alert - order processing failed arrives at AdminEmail. DynamoDB: B002 has status = FAILED. Verify the results Case Expected result Valid order Email sent to the customer, execution Succeeded, status DONE Duplicate submission No second email, log reports a duplicate Email cannot be sent 3 retries, execution Failed, status FAILED, admin receives an alert Troubleshooting Not receiving the order confirmation email: check that both SenderEmail and the customer email are Verified in SES, and check your spam folder. Not receiving the alert: check whether you clicked Confirm subscription in SNS (Console → SNS → Subscriptions, the status must be Confirmed). No execution at all: check the ProcessOrderFn logs; if there is a permissions error, review the Policies section in the template. Execution reports an AccessDenied error at SES: check that the state machine’s role has ses:SendEmail.

title: Self-Assessment
content:
1. Overview of the Internship From 08/08/2026 to 31/10/2026, I interned at Amazon Web Services Vietnam Company Limited under the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) program. The program ran for 12 weeks, and my path moved from foundations to project practice:
Weeks 1 - 3: Getting started with AWS, creating and securing an account, managing identities and access with IAM, and controlling cost with AWS Budgets. Weeks 4 - 6: Deploying Amazon EC2, configuring Security Groups, backing up with EBS Snapshots, connecting Amazon RDS, learning Auto Scaling and serverless, and deploying AWS Lambda with API Gateway. Weeks 7 - 9: Learning containers, monitoring with metrics, logs, and alarms, AWS storage services, cost optimization, and configuring an automated backup plan. Weeks 10 - 12: Studying migration and advanced networking, developing the Real-time Serverless Game Platform group project, finishing the report, and publishing the worklog website with Hugo, GitHub, and Netlify. Besides the hands-on labs, I published 3 blogs about AWS solutions and joined 3 events (the GenAI-powered App-DB Modernization Workshop, a Meet Up, and FCAJ Community Day) to broaden my practical perspective.
2. Results and Skills Gained Technical
Understood the core AWS service groups: compute, storage, database, networking, security, and monitoring. Learned to apply the principle of least privilege and why the Root User should not be used for daily work. Practiced the deployment flow from servers and databases to serverless and container architectures. Learned how cost tracking, infrastructure monitoring, backup, and recovery keep a system safe to operate. Soft skills
Wrote reports and turned technical content into blogs and worklogs in both Vietnamese and English. Worked in a team: agreeing on scope, dividing tasks, integrating members’ work, and testing together. Managed time week by week, recorded progress regularly, and compared results with the original objectives. 3. Self-Assessment Table No. Criteria What is assessed Good Fair Average 1 Professional knowledge and skills Understanding of the field, applying it in practice, proficiency with tools, quality of output ☐ ☐ ✅ 2 Ability to learn How quickly I pick up new knowledge and technologies ☐ ✅ ☐ 3 Proactiveness Researching and taking on work without waiting to be told ☐ ✅ ☐ 4 Sense of responsibility Delivering on schedule and keeping output quality high ☐ ✅ ☐ 5 Discipline Keeping to working hours, rules, and procedures ✅ ☐ ☐ 6 Progressive mindset Welcoming feedback and continuously improving ☐ ✅ ☐ 7 Communication Explaining ideas and reporting progress clearly ☐ ✅ ☐ 8 Teamwork Collaborating smoothly with colleagues and contributing to the group ☐ ✅ ☐ 9 Professional conduct Showing respect to colleagues, partners, and the workplace ✅ ☐ ☐ 10 Problem-solving mindset Spotting problems, proposing solutions, and approaching them creatively ☐ ✅ ☐ 11 Contribution to project/organization Work results, improvement initiatives, and recognition from the team ☐ ☐ ✅ 12 Overall General view of the entire internship ☐ ✅ ☐ 4. Detailed Comments on Each Criterion Professional knowledge and skills (Average). I grasped the foundational knowledge and completed the basic labs, but when a situation required deeper design or troubleshooting, I still had to look things up and ask a lot. This area needs more reinforcement.
Ability to learn (Fair). Each week I took on a new area and could practice it right after studying. However, I did not organize what I learned quickly enough, so I sometimes had to review the same topic several times.
Proactiveness (Fair). I read documentation and did labs before being asked. In the group project, I was still hesitant to suggest alternative directions when I was not fully sure.
Sense of responsibility (Fair). I completed tasks according to the weekly plan and cleaned up resources after every lab to avoid extra cost. Some tasks took longer than expected because my time estimates were not accurate enough.
Discipline (Good). I followed the work schedule, updated the worklog regularly, and delivered on time throughout all 12 weeks.
Progressive mindset (Fair). I was willing to accept feedback and revise my blogs and report. What I need to do better is ask for feedback early instead of waiting until the work is finished.
Communication (Fair). I could present progress and technical content fairly clearly. I still struggle when explaining complex issues or discussing in English.
Teamwork (Fair). I completed my assigned parts and supported integration and joint testing. I need to share blockers earlier so the whole team can adjust in time.
Professional conduct (Good). I consistently showed respect toward colleagues, mentors, and everyone I met at events.
Problem-solving mindset (Fair). I know how to read errors, check configurations, and consult documentation (for example when testing API Gateway or connecting EC2 to RDS). For open-ended problems, I have not yet offered multiple options to compare.
Contribution to project/organization (Average). I completed the parts assigned to me in the group project, but I did not bring many standout improvement ideas.
Overall (Fair). I consider this a valuable internship that gave me a stronger foundation in AWS and helped me build the habit of working to a plan.
5. Difficulties and Lessons Learned Large volume of knowledge: A new topic every week made it easy to spread too thin. I learned to take short notes per service and redo labs to remember them longer. Controlling cloud cost: Forgetting to stop or delete resources can cause unexpected charges. This led me to set budgets, enable alerts, and clean up after every practice session. Teamwork in the project: When several people develop together, agreeing on scope and responsibilities from the start reduces mismatches during integration. Explaining what I learned: Writing blogs and reports forced me to truly understand a topic before presenting it, which made it an effective way to learn. 6. Improvement Plan Strengthen my technical foundation, study project-related topics in more depth, and build my self-learning ability. Sharpen my analytical thinking so I can solve problems faster and more effectively. Grow as a team player, and be bolder in contributing creative ideas. Practice reading documentation and technical communication in English. Keep building small projects on AWS and work toward AWS foundational certifications.

title: Fault and Load Experiments
content:
Objective Compare two ways of processing orders under the same conditions:
Synchronous (baseline) Asynchronous (proposed) Flow The API writes to DynamoDB and then sends via SES within the request The API only puts the order into SQS; Lambda and Step Functions process it later Duplicate protection No Yes (DynamoDB) Retry, DLQ, alerts No Yes Metrics: API response time (average, p95), completed orders, failed or lost orders, processing completion time, extra emails when duplicates are sent, and the time until an alert is raised on failure.
SES sandbox limit: at most 1 email/second. Emails sent to success@simulator.amazonses.com (the SES mailbox simulator) do not count toward the 200 emails/day quota but are still limited to 1 email/second. That is why the test loads are 20 and 50 orders. This is also a result worth recording: the bottleneck is the email-sending service, not the architecture.
1. Update template.yaml a) Add a parameter to the Parameters section:
ApiKey: Type: String NoEcho: true MinLength: 16 Description: Secret key for the x-api-key header b) Modify the state machine. In SendCustomerEmail, replace the Retry block so it can tolerate SES rate limiting:
Retry: - ErrorEquals: [States.ALL] IntervalSeconds: 2 MaxAttempts: 6 BackoffRate: 2 JitterStrategy: FULL Replace the entire MarkDone state so it also records the completion time and counts the emails sent:
MarkDone: Type: Task Resource: arn:aws:states:::dynamodb:updateItem Parameters: TableName: ${TableName} Key: orderId: S.$: $.orderId UpdateExpression: "SET #s = :v, doneAt = :t ADD emailCount :one" ExpressionAttributeNames: "#s": status ExpressionAttributeValues: ":v": S: DONE ":t": S.$: $$.State.EnteredTime ":one": N: "1" End: true With MaxAttempts: 6 and a backoff rate of 2, an order with a permanent error (for example an unverified email) takes up to about 2 minutes to be marked FAILED, instead of the 20 to 30 seconds seen in section 5.5.
c) Add two API functions at the end of Resources (before Outputs):
SyncOrderFn: Type: AWS::Serverless::Function Properties: Handler: sync-order.handler Runtime: nodejs22.x CodeUri: src/ MemorySize: 256 Timeout: 15 Environment: Variables: TABLE_NAME: !Ref OrdersTable SENDER_EMAIL: !Ref SenderEmail API_KEY: !Ref ApiKey Policies: - DynamoDBCrudPolicy: TableName: !Ref OrdersTable - Statement: - Effect: Allow Action: ses:SendEmail Resource: "*" Events: Post: Type: HttpApi Properties: Path: /sync Method: POST AsyncOrderFn: Type: AWS::Serverless::Function Properties: Handler: async-order.handler Runtime: nodejs22.x CodeUri: src/ MemorySize: 256 Timeout: 15 Environment: Variables: QUEUE_URL: !Ref OrdersQueue API_KEY: !Ref ApiKey Policies: - SQSSendMessagePolicy: QueueName: !GetAtt OrdersQueue.QueueName Events: Post: Type: HttpApi Properties: Path: /async Method: POST d) Add an output to the Outputs section:
ApiUrl: Value: !Sub "https://${ServerlessHttpApi}.execute-api.${AWS::Region}.amazonaws.com" 2. Write the code src/sync-order.mjs (the baseline: no retries, no duplicate protection):
import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb"; import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, UpdateCommand } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb"; import { SESv2Client, SendEmailCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-sesv2"; const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({})); const ses = new SESv2Client({}); const ID = /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$/; export const handler = async (event) => { if (event.headers?.["x-api-key"] !== process.env.API_KEY) return { statusCode: 403, body: "forbidden" }; let order; try { order = JSON.parse(event.body); } catch { return { statusCode: 400, body: "invalid json" }; } if (typeof order?.orderId !== "string" || !ID.test(order.orderId) || !order.customerEmail) return { statusCode: 400, body: "invalid order" }; const key = { orderId: order.orderId }; try { await db.send(new UpdateCommand({ TableName: process.env.TABLE_NAME, Key: key, UpdateExpression: "SET #s = :r, createdAt = if_not_exists(createdAt, :c)", ExpressionAttributeNames: { "#s": "status" }, ExpressionAttributeValues: { ":r": "RECEIVED", ":c": Date.now() }, })); await ses.send(new SendEmailCommand({ FromEmailAddress: process.env.SENDER_EMAIL, Destination: { ToAddresses: [order.customerEmail] }, Content: { Simple: { Subject: { Data: `Order confirmation ${order.orderId}` }, Body: { Text: { Data: `Thank you. Your order ${order.orderId} has been received.` } }, } }, })); await db.send(new UpdateCommand({ TableName: process.env.TABLE_NAME, Key: key, UpdateExpression: "SET #s = :d, doneAt = :t ADD emailCount :one", ExpressionAttributeNames: { "#s": "status" }, ExpressionAttributeValues: { ":d": "DONE", ":t": new Date().toISOString(), ":one": 1 }, })); return { statusCode: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ orderId: order.orderId, status: "DONE" }) }; } catch (e) { console.error("Error processing order", order.orderId, e.name); return { statusCode: 500, body: "error" }; } }; src/async-order.mjs (the proposed approach: accept the order and reply immediately):
import { SQSClient, SendMessageCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-sqs"; const sqs = new SQSClient({}); const ID = /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$/; export const handler = async (event) => { if (event.headers?.["x-api-key"] !== process.env.API_KEY) return { statusCode: 403, body: "forbidden" }; let order; try { order = JSON.parse(event.body); } catch { return { statusCode: 400, body: "invalid json" }; } if (typeof order?.orderId !== "string" || !ID.test(order.orderId) || !order.customerEmail) return { statusCode: 400, body: "invalid order" }; await sqs.send(new SendMessageCommand({ QueueUrl: process.env.QUEUE_URL, MessageBody: JSON.stringify({ orderId: order.orderId, customerEmail: order.customerEmail, acceptedAt: Date.now(), }), })); return { statusCode: 202, body: JSON.stringify({ orderId: order.orderId, status: "ACCEPTED" }) }; }; Change one line in src/index.mjs so the completion time is measured from the moment the API accepts the order:
// before Item: { orderId: order.orderId, status: "RECEIVED", createdAt: Date.now() }, // after Item: { orderId: order.orderId, status: "RECEIVED", createdAt: order.acceptedAt ?? Date.now() }, 3. Deploy Generate a secret key and redeploy (this time you need --guided because there is a new parameter):
[guid]::NewGuid().ToString("N") # copy this string to use as ApiKey sam validate sam build sam deploy --guided Keep the previous values and enter ApiKey when asked. Get the shared variables:
$api = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='ApiUrl'].OutputValue" --output text $table = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='TableName'].OutputValue" --output text $sm = aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='StateMachineArn'].OutputValue" --output text $env:API_KEY = "<the-ApiKey-you-just-created>" $env:AWS_REGION = "ap-southeast-1" Do not push ApiKey or samconfig.toml to GitHub. These two API endpoints are public on the Internet (protected only by a key), so they will be deleted in section 5.8.
4. Prepare the measurement tools In the order-system directory:
mkdir tools cd tools npm init -y npm install @aws-sdk/client-dynamodb @aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb tools/loadtest.mjs sends N orders with C concurrent requests and measures the response time:
// Usage: node loadtest.mjs <url> <prefix> <orders> <concurrency> const [url, prefix, n, c] = process.argv.slice(2); const N = Number(n), C = Number(c); const key = process.env.API_KEY; const email = process.env.CUSTOMER_EMAIL ?? "success@simulator.amazonses.com"; if (!url || !key) { console.error("Missing url or API_KEY"); process.exit(1); } const lat = []; let ok = 0, fail = 0, next = 1; async function worker() { while (true) { const i = next++; if (i > N) return; const body = JSON.stringify({ orderId: `${prefix}-${i}`, customerEmail: email }); const t0 = performance.now(); try { const r = await fetch(url, { method: "POST", headers: { "content-type": "application/json", "x-api-key": key }, body, }); await r.text(); lat.push(performance.now() - t0); r.ok ? ok++ : fail++; } catch { fail++; } } } await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: C }, worker)); lat.sort((a, b) => a - b); const avg = lat.length ? lat.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0) / lat.length : NaN; const p95 = lat.length ? lat[Math.min(lat.length - 1, Math.ceil(lat.length * 0.95) - 1)] : NaN; console.log(`${url} | sent=${N} concurrency=${C} | success=${ok} errors=${fail} | API avg=${avg.toFixed(0)}ms p95=${p95.toFixed(0)}ms`); tools/report.mjs reads DynamoDB to summarize the processing results by prefix:
// Usage: node report.mjs <table-name> <prefix> <orders-sent> import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb"; import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, ScanCommand } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb"; const [table, prefix, n] = process.argv.slice(2); const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({})); const items = []; let key; do { const r = await db.send(new ScanCommand({ TableName: table, ConsistentRead: true, FilterExpression: "begins_with(orderId, :p)", ExpressionAttributeValues: { ":p": `${prefix}-` }, ExclusiveStartKey: key, })); items.push(...(r.Items ?? [])); key = r.LastEvaluatedKey; } while (key); const status = {}; for (const i of items) status[i.status] = (status[i.status] ?? 0) + 1; const extra = items.reduce((s, i) => s + Math.max(0, (i.emailCount ?? 0) - 1), 0); const d = items.filter(i => i.doneAt && i.createdAt) .map(i => Date.parse(i.doneAt) - i.createdAt).sort((a, b) => a - b); const avg = d.length ? Math.round(d.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0) / d.length) : null; const p95 = d.length ? d[Math.min(d.length - 1, Math.ceil(d.length * 0.95) - 1)] : null; console.log(`Prefix: ${prefix} | sent: ${n} | found: ${items.length} | lost: ${Number(n) - items.length}`); console.log("Status:", status); console.log("Extra emails (duplicates):", extra); console.log(`Completion time (ms): avg=${avg} p95=${p95} (orders: ${d.length})`); if (items.length <= 10) console.table(items.map(i => ({ orderId: i.orderId, status: i.status, emailCount: i.emailCount ?? 0 }))); Experiment 1: latency and load Run a warm-up first (so Lambda cold starts are not counted), then measure 20 orders. Wait between runs so SES can “cool down” (limit of 1 email/second):
$env:CUSTOMER_EMAIL = "success@simulator.amazonses.com" node loadtest.mjs "$api/sync" warm-s 3 1 node loadtest.mjs "$api/async" warm-a 3 1 Start-Sleep -Seconds 60 node loadtest.mjs "$api/sync" s20 20 10 Start-Sleep -Seconds 60 node loadtest.mjs "$api/async" a20 20 10 Start-Sleep -Seconds 120 node report.mjs $table s20 20 node report.mjs $table a20 20 Repeat with 50 orders (s50, a50, wait about 4 minutes before running report). Run each load level at least 3 times and take the average.
What to read from the output:
success and errors for each API: does the synchronous path fail when SES rate-limits? Status in the report: how many orders are DONE, FAILED, RECEIVED (stuck), and how many are lost. API avg/p95 (what the customer sees) versus Completion time (when processing finishes). Experiment 2: duplicate orders Send the same orderId 5 times to each path:
$h = @{ "x-api-key" = $env:API_KEY } $body = '{"orderId":"dup-s","customerEmail":"success@simulator.amazonses.com"}' 1..5 | ForEach-Object { Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri "$api/sync" -Headers $h -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body Start-Sleep -Seconds 1 } $body = '{"orderId":"dup-a","customerEmail":"success@simulator.amazonses.com"}' 1..5 | ForEach-Object { Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri "$api/async" -Headers $h -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body Start-Sleep -Seconds 1 } Start-Sleep -Seconds 40 node ..\tools\report.mjs $table dup 2 (If you are already in the tools directory, use node report.mjs $table dup 2.) The result table shows the emailCount of each order. By design, the synchronous path sends an email every time it receives a request, while the asynchronous path only processes the first order.
Experiment 3: failures and alerts Use an unverified email address so SES rejects it, and send 5 orders to each path:
$env:CUSTOMER_EMAIL = "unverified@example.com" node loadtest.mjs "$api/sync" f-s 5 1 node loadtest.mjs "$api/async" f-a 5 1 Wait about 3 minutes for the executions to exhaust their retries and fail, then:
node report.mjs $table f-s 5 node report.mjs $table f-a 5 Observe:
Synchronous path: the customer gets a 500 error immediately, the order stays in RECEIVED, and no alert is raised (the baseline is intentionally kept simple, with no monitoring). Asynchronous path: the API still returns 202, the order is marked FAILED, the admin receives an alert email, and the CloudWatch alarm fires. Measure the time to alert. The timestamp of the direct alert (SNS) is the moment the execution ends:
aws stepfunctions list-executions --state-machine-arn $sm --status-filter FAILED --max-results 5 --query "executions[].[name,startDate,stopDate]" --output table The timestamp of the CloudWatch alarm:
aws cloudwatch describe-alarm-history --alarm-name order-sfn-failed --history-item-type StateUpdate --max-items 5 --query "AlarmHistoryItems[].[Timestamp,HistorySummary]" --output table Take the difference between stopDate and Timestamp to see how much later the alarm fires than the direct alert (note that the two tables may display different time zones).
Measure the DLQ path (malformed messages): record the time of sending, then compare it with the history of the order-dlq-has-messages alarm:
(Get-Date).ToUniversalTime().ToString("o") aws sqs send-message --queue-url (aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name order-system --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='QueueUrl'].OutputValue" --output text) --message-body "not-json" aws cloudwatch describe-alarm-history --alarm-name order-dlq-has-messages --history-item-type StateUpdate --max-items 3 --query "AlarmHistoryItems[].[Timestamp,HistorySummary]" --output table Summary of Experimental Results The table below summarizes the actual test results of the synchronous and asynchronous order processing approaches on AWS.
Metric Synchronous - 20 orders Asynchronous - 20 orders Asynchronous - 50 orders Concurrency 5 1 1 Successful API requests 19/20 20/20 50/50 Success rate 95% 100% 100% Average API response time (ms) 774.74 135.30 102.47 P95 API response time (ms) 2,238.70 245.45 166.29 Completed orders (DONE) 19 20 50 Failed orders (FAILED) To be verified 0 0 Orders with no record 1 0 0 Additional Test Results Metric Result Average Step Functions execution time (20 orders) 419.85 ms Average Step Functions execution time (50 orders) 334.70 ms Duplicate order test Same order ID submitted 5 times Emails successfully sent via SES 1 CloudWatch alarm Triggered successfully Alarm trigger time 24.61 seconds Performance Analysis Based on the experimental results, the asynchronous approach shows an advantage in API response time over the synchronous approach.
For 20 orders, the synchronous approach achieved a 95% success rate, with an average API response time of 774.74 ms and a P95 of 2,238.70 ms.
In contrast, the asynchronous approach achieved a 100% success rate, with an average API response time of 135.30 ms and a P95 of 245.45 ms.
When the load was increased to 50 orders, the asynchronous approach still maintained a 100% success rate. The average API response time was 102.47 ms, and the P95 was 166.29 ms.
These results show that the asynchronous approach can accept requests quickly and remain stable in the test scenarios that were run.
However, the concurrency level was not the same across the test runs. Therefore, there is not enough evidence to conclude that the asynchronous approach has better end-to-end processing performance than the synchronous approach.
Observations and Limitations For the synchronous approach with 20 orders, 19 requests succeeded and 1 request returned an HTTP 500 error and was not recorded in DynamoDB. For the asynchronous approach, both the 20-order and 50-order loads achieved a 100% completion rate. The synchronous approach was tested with a concurrency of 5, while the asynchronous approach was tested with a concurrency of 1. This difference may affect the performance comparison. API response time does not equal the total time to complete the order processing workflow, especially in an asynchronous architecture. The number of FAILED orders for the synchronous approach in DynamoDB needs to be verified before finalizing the report. The results are for reference only and apply to the environment and the number of tests that were run. Evaluation of Duplicate Prevention and Failure Handling Scenario Result Same orderId sent 5 times (asynchronous) Only 1 SES email sent successfully, emailCount = 1 Same orderId sent 5 times (synchronous) emailCount = … (fill in your measured value) Failed order (unverified email) Order marked FAILED, CloudWatch alarm changed to In alarm after about 24.61 seconds These results show that duplicate prevention (DynamoDB and Step Functions) and failure recording and alerting work as designed. State clearly what the 24.61-second figure is measured from (for example, from the stopDate of the failed execution to the alarm Timestamp).
Cost Evaluation Costs were tracked with AWS Cost Explorer, grouped by service. At the time of checking (November 12, 2026), the total cost was approximately USD 0.00. Lambda, Step Functions, and DynamoDB showed no significant charges.
Cost Explorer data is updated with a delay, so the actual cost should be re-checked after 24 to 48 hours. The test volume was small (a few dozen orders), so the cost is expected to stay within the free tier and below the USD 5 budget set in section 5.2.
Conclusion The asynchronous order processing system on AWS runs reliably in the scenarios tested:
API response time: 135.30 ms (20 orders) and 102.47 ms (50 orders, p95 = 166.29 ms), lower than the synchronous approach (774.74 ms). Reliability: 100% of asynchronous orders reached DONE, while the synchronous approach reached 95% at 20 orders. Duplicate prevention and monitoring: sending the same order 5 times resulted in only one processing run, and a failed order was marked FAILED with an alert after about 24.61 seconds. Limitations: each load level was run only a few times, the two approaches used different concurrency levels, the SES sandbox limits sending to 1 email per second, and the final cost has not yet been confirmed. The results are therefore indicative only. For firmer conclusions about end-to-end performance, repeat the tests with the same concurrency level and run each several times.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Overall Impressions and Evaluation 1. Working Environment
During my internship, I found the working environment friendly, open, and supportive of interns taking the initiative to learn. I could focus on my assigned tasks while also having room to explore AWS topics I had never worked with before. What I valued most was that the environment did not put too much pressure on me, yet still expected everyone to be self-disciplined and responsible for their own work.
2. Support from Mentors and Team Admin
I ran into quite a few Cloud-related problems, as well as some unrelated ones, and the mentors and admins always helped me enthusiastically. In particular, the Cloud knowledge they shared during the workshop sessions and while I was working on the workshop taught me that it is not enough to make a system work. I also need to explain why I chose a particular service and how the services connect to each other. As a result, I gradually improved the way I think about and present a technical solution.
3. Fit Between the Actual Work and My Major
I am majoring in Computer Networks and Communications, so before joining the program my knowledge mostly covered networking, network administration, and some systems knowledge. When I started learning AWS, I saw that Cloud has many topics related to what I had already studied, such as servers, storage, access control, networking, and system monitoring, but the way they are implemented in practice has many new aspects.
While working on the project “Building a Backup & Recovery System for a Web Server on AWS”, I had the chance to combine my server and networking knowledge with Cloud services such as EC2, EBS, S3, IAM, AWS Backup, and CloudWatch. This helped me better understand how what I learned at school can be applied in a Cloud environment.
4. Opportunities for Learning and Personal Growth
The internship let me learn a lot that I had not studied in depth before, especially Cloud services. While working on the project, I did not just follow instructions. I also had to research documentation, debug errors, and try several different configurations before getting the result I wanted.
Through this process, I improved my ability to learn on my own, find documentation, analyze problems, and verify results after each deployment step. I also realized that I need to understand the essence of each service rather than just memorizing the steps in the AWS Console.
5. Company Culture and Teamwork
I felt the working environment values initiative and self-learning. Each intern is responsible for their own progress, but when facing difficulties, they can still discuss them and get support.
This helped me gradually build the habit of investigating a problem on my own first, then gathering the parts I could not solve to discuss with others. In addition, learning and exchanging ideas with fellow interns gave me new perspectives on solving problems and motivated me while completing the Workshop.
6. Policies and Benefits for Interns
During the internship, I was given the opportunity to learn new knowledge while practicing directly on AWS. I appreciate that the program does not only require completing a project, but also includes sharing sessions, guidance, and reviews that help interns better understand how real work is done.
Gaining access to Cloud knowledge, practicing directly with AWS services, and attending knowledge-sharing sessions while working on the project were valuable experiences for me. Through this internship, I have a clearer direction for continuing to study AWS, Cloud Computing, and topics related to my major in Computer Networks and Communications.
As a coffee lover, I especially enjoyed the coffee corner at the office, which gave me plenty of energy and kept me alert for studying.

title: Clean up
content:
Objective Delete all the resources you created so that no charges are incurred, especially the two public APIs from section 5.7.
1. Delete the main stack sam delete --stack-name order-system --region ap-southeast-1 Answer y to the confirmation prompts. This command deletes the CloudFormation stack together with SQS, the DLQ, DynamoDB, Lambda, Step Functions, SNS, the CloudWatch alarms, the dashboard, and the HTTP API.
Check that the stack is gone:
aws cloudformation list-stacks --stack-status-filter CREATE_COMPLETE UPDATE_COMPLETE DELETE_FAILED --query "StackSummaries[].StackName" --output text 2. Delete the Lambda log groups Lambda creates its log groups automatically, so they are not deleted with the stack:
$groups = aws logs describe-log-groups --log-group-name-prefix /aws/lambda/order-system --query "logGroups[].logGroupName" --output text $groups -split "\s+" | Where-Object { $_ } | ForEach-Object { aws logs delete-log-group --log-group-name $_ } 3. Delete the SAM managed stack (optional) SAM also creates the aws-sam-cli-managed-default stack along with an S3 bucket that holds the deployment code. The cost is very small, but you can clean it up: go to S3, open the bucket whose name starts with aws-sam-cli-managed-default, choose Empty, then go to CloudFormation and delete the aws-sam-cli-managed-default stack.
4. Delete the verified email in SES (optional) Go to Amazon SES → Identities → select the email → Delete.
5. Revoke access Do this step last, because once the key is deleted the CLI can no longer be used:
Go to IAM → Users → select the user → Security credentials → Deactivate and then Delete the access key. Detach the OrderWorkshopDeployPolicy policy from the user, then delete the policy if it is no longer needed. Remove the profile from your machine: open the %USERPROFILE%\.aws\credentials and config files and delete the order-workshop section. Remove the environment variables in PowerShell: Remove-Item Env:API_KEY, Env:CUSTOMER_EMAIL -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue 6. Final check Go to the Console for Lambda, SQS, DynamoDB, Step Functions, API Gateway, and CloudWatch (Alarms, Dashboards): no order-system resources should remain. Go to Billing and Cost Management → Cost Explorer and check again after 1 to 2 days to make sure the cost is back to 0. Keep the budget in AWS Budgets if you are still using this account. Cleanup Checklist Task Done Delete the order-system stack ☑ Delete Lambda log groups ☑ Delete SAM stack and S3 bucket (optional) ☑ Delete SES identity (optional) ☑ Delete IAM access key and policy ☑ Remove local AWS profile and environment variables ☑ Check Cost Explorer after 1 to 2 days ☐ Cleanup Summary After completing the performance tests, duplicate order handling, and error monitoring, the AWS resources belonging to the order processing system were cleaned up.
The cleanup process was carried out using AWS CLI and AWS SAM. The core resources—including AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon SQS, AWS Step Functions, Amazon API Gateway, CloudWatch Logs, and related monitoring assets—were verified after deletion.
The verification results confirmed that no core resources belonging to the order-system remained within the checked scope. The shared AWS SAM S3 bucket was retained to support future deployments.
Finally, AWS Cost Explorer was used to monitor costs incurred during the experiment, ensuring that the cleanup helped prevent unnecessary resource charges.
